nameStory: The Buckler Dory gets its name from its shield-like body shape, resembling the round buckler shields carried by medieval warriors. The word 'dory' comes from the French 'dorée' meaning 'golden,' referring to the yellowish coloration many dory species display.
description: The Buckler Dory is a deep-sea fish with a dramatically flattened, disc-like body that looks almost coin-shaped when viewed head-on. This unusual fish has large eyes and a protrusible mouth that can shoot forward to catch prey. They're typically found in very deep waters off New England's coast, far below where recreational divers venture. Adult Buckler Dories can reach substantial sizes, though they're rarely seen due to their deep-water habitat.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely compressed, almost pancake-flat body that's nearly circular when viewed from the side, feeling rigid and bony to the touch

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large, tube-like mouth that can extend outward dramatically when feeding, with a somewhat rubbery texture around the lips

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, prominent dorsal and anal fins with spiny rays that feel sharp and sturdy, extending well along the body's edge

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Silvery body with a metallic sheen that reflects light, often with darker vertical bands or spots

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large fish reaching impressive sizes, with a hefty, solid feel when handled despite the flattened appearance

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Deep ocean waters well offshore, typically caught by commercial fishermen rather than recreational anglers

habitat: Buckler Dories inhabit the deep continental shelf and slope waters off New England's coast, typically found at depths far below recreational fishing zones. They prefer the cold, deep waters of the North Atlantic where they cruise near the bottom hunting for smaller fish and invertebrates. These fish are occasionally caught as bycatch by commercial fishing operations working the deep offshore grounds.

seasonality.spring: Deep-water commercial fishing may occasionally bring up Buckler Dories as temperatures begin to warm, though sightings remain extremely rare.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season to encounter this species through commercial fishing operations working the deeper offshore waters during peak fishing season.
seasonality.fall: Continued occasional catches possible as commercial boats work the deep waters, though the species remains elusive to most observers.
seasonality.winter: Least likely to be observed as harsh weather limits deep-water fishing operations that might encounter this species.

funFact: Despite looking like they'd be clumsy swimmers with their pancake-flat bodies, Buckler Dories are actually ambush predators that can shoot their mouths forward like a telescope to snatch unsuspecting prey - their unusual shape makes them nearly invisible when viewed head-on!
confusionNotes: With only 4 recorded observations in New England, the Buckler Dory is unlikely to be confused with anything else due to its rarity, but its flattened body might remind some of a large flounder - remember that flounders have both eyes on one side of their head, while dories have normal eye placement.
contextualKnowledge: The Buckler Dory belongs to the same family as the more famous John Dory, and like its relative, it's considered excellent eating in European cuisine, though it's far too rare in New England waters to be of commercial importance here.
compareHints: The Buckler Dory is the only member of its genus recorded in New England waters, making it unique in the region. Compared to its more famous relative the John Dory, the Buckler Dory typically grows larger and has a more pronounced shield-like body shape. Both species share the characteristic compressed body and extendable mouth, but the Buckler Dory's extreme rarity in New England waters makes any sighting particularly noteworthy.
